title: Fractions in Year 6: A Guide for Parents Who Do Not Speak German
audience: parents of Year 6 pupils at a Bavarian Gymnasium who do not speak German
hook: Your child comes home with a maths exercise book full of words you have never heard: «Zähler», «Nenner», «kürzen». This video gives you the maths and the words in a little over ten minutes.
keyTakeaway: You do not need German to help with fractions. Learn the handful of words the school uses, let your child explain the pictures to you, and use everyday things at home.
learningObjectives: Know what the Bavarian curriculum (LehrplanPLUS) expects in topic M6 1.1 and why it matters for later years
Understand the four core ideas: share of a whole, expanding and reducing, comparing, fractions as numbers
Recognise the German school terms your child brings home and what they mean
Spot the five typical mistakes and know how to correct them
Help at home in ten minutes a day, even without German

youtube.title: Fractions in Year 6 at a German Gymnasium: Guide for Non-German-Speaking Parents (Bavaria)
youtube.description:
For parents who do not speak German and whose child attends Jahrgangsstufe 6 at a Gymnasium in Bavaria. What the LehrplanPLUS curriculum expects in topic M6 1.1 Bruchteile und Bruchzahlen, the four core ideas in pictures (share of a whole, erweitern and kürzen, Hauptnenner, Zahlengerade), the German school words your child brings home with their English meaning, five common mistakes, and how to practise at home in ten minutes without speaking German.

German terms in this video: Bruch, Zähler, Nenner, Bruchstrich, Anteil, das Ganze, erweitern, kürzen, vollständig gekürzt, gleichnamig, Hauptnenner, Zahlengerade, Prozent, natürliche Zahlen, rationale Zahlen, Schulaufgabe, Stegreifaufgabe, Grundwissen.

The German version for parents (Eltern-Lektion) and the lesson for children (Lektion) are on this channel as well. Curriculum: LehrplanPLUS Gymnasium Bayern, Mathematik 6, Lernbereich 1.1.
youtube.pinnedComment: Which German school term puzzles you most? Ask in the comments and we will explain it in the next video.

chapters.title: What this is about
chapters.goal: You know what the curriculum expects and why this topic matters for the years ahead.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Fractions: a guide for international parents
scenes.narration: Your child comes home from a Bavarian Gymnasium with a maths exercise book full of words you have never heard. «Zähler», «Nenner», «kürzen». The maths behind them is fractions. Chances are you know fractions well; the new part is the German vocabulary. This video gives you both in a little over ten minutes: what the Bavarian curriculum expects in Year six, «Jahrgangsstufe sechs», pupils aged about eleven to twelve, grade six in many countries, the four ideas at the heart of it, the German words your child will use, the typical mistakes, and how to help at home without speaking German.

scenes.onScreenTitle: The curriculum: M6 1.1 Bruchteile und Bruchzahlen
bullets: LehrplanPLUS: the Bavarian curriculum for Gymnasium
Topic M6 1.1, about 13 lessons
First part of a 68-lesson block on rational numbers
scenes.narration: The Bavarian curriculum is called the «LehrplanPLUS». In mathematics for Year six the first topic is «Bruchteile und Bruchzahlen», fractional parts and fractions. It is planned for about thirteen lessons and opens a large block on rational numbers, «rationale Zahlen», that takes sixty-eight lessons, more than half of the maths lessons the curriculum plans for the year. Decimals, adding and multiplying fractions all build on these first thirteen lessons.

bullets: Read and draw shares: circles and rectangles
Expand and reduce; find a common denominator
Compare fractions; per cent as another notation
Fractions as numbers on the number line, also negative
scenes.narration: Four competences are listed. First: read a share from a picture and draw it, with circles and rectangles, and find the part and the whole. Second: understand that expanding and reducing a fraction, «erweitern» and «kürzen», do not change its value, and find a common denominator, the «Hauptnenner». Third: compare fractions and know per cent as another way of writing a fraction. Fourth: place fractions as numbers on the number line, the «Zahlengerade», including negative ones. Tests on this topic often draw on these four points, but the exact selection is up to the teacher.

chapters.title: The four core ideas, in pictures
chapters.goal: You know the pictures the school uses so you can talk about them with your child.

scenes.narration: In Bavaria, fractions are taught through pictures first and rules second. Four pictures carry the whole topic: a circle cut into equal parts, the same circle cut finer, two fractions side by side, and the number line. If your child can explain these four pictures to you, the rules will follow. Let us look at each one, with the German words the teacher will use.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Idea 1: a share of a whole
scenes.narration: Idea one. A circle is cut into eight equal parts, and three of them are coloured. That is three eighths, in German «drei Achtel». The fraction is written with a bar, the «Bruchstrich». Above it stands the number of coloured parts, the «Zähler», the numerator. Below it stands the number of equal parts in the whole, the «Nenner», the denominator. The parts must be equal. A circle cut unevenly is not a fraction picture, and teachers will usually point that out.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Idea 2: expanding does not change the value
scenes.narration: Idea two. Cut every piece once more. Now there are sixteen parts and six are coloured: six sixteenths. The amount of circle has not changed. Multiplying top and bottom by the same number is called «erweitern», expanding. Dividing both by the same number is «kürzen», reducing. When no further division is possible the fraction is «vollständig gekürzt», fully reduced. Your child will hear these three words almost every lesson, and the picture is the proof behind them.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Idea 3: comparing with a common denominator
scenes.narration: Idea three. Which is larger, two thirds or three quarters? The pictures help, but a reliable method is to give both fractions the same denominator. Two thirds becomes eight twelfths, three quarters becomes nine twelfths. Fractions with the same denominator are called «gleichnamig», and the smallest shared denominator is the «Hauptnenner», the lowest common denominator. Now the comparison is easy: nine twelfths is larger. Later in the year this same step is what makes adding fractions possible.

Idea four, which is easy to overlook. A fraction is not only a piece of pizza. It is a number with a place on the number line, the «Zahlengerade». One half sits exactly between zero and one. Negative fractions sit to the left of zero: minus three quarters lies between minus one and minus one half. Your child learns three names for number sets. The natural numbers, «natürliche Zahlen», start at one in Bavarian schools. With zero and the negatives they become the whole numbers, «ganze Zahlen». With the fractions they become the rational numbers, «rationale Zahlen». Between any two rational numbers there is always another one.

chapters.title: The words your child brings home
chapters.goal: You recognise the German school terms and know what they mean.

scenes.narration: Here are the words in one place, so you can keep up when your child talks about homework. There are three groups: the parts of a fraction, the verbs for what you do with fractions, and the words for the tests themselves. You do not need to pronounce them well. You need to recognise them when your child says them, and know what they mean.

bullets: Bruch = fraction; Bruchstrich = fraction bar
Zähler = numerator (top); Nenner = denominator (bottom)
Anteil = share; Bruchteil = part; Ganze = whole
Zahlengerade = number line; Prozent = per cent
scenes.narration: The fraction itself is «der Bruch». The bar is «der Bruchstrich». The top number is «der Zähler», which literally means the counter, because it counts the parts. The bottom number is «der Nenner», the namer, because it names the kind of part: eighths, twelfths. The share is «der Anteil», the part is «der Bruchteil», and the whole is «das Ganze». Many word problems hinge on that last one: three quarters of what? A memory aid: «Zähler» counts, «Nenner» names.

bullets: erweitern = expand; kürzen = reduce
gleichnamig = same denominator; Hauptnenner = lowest common denominator
Schulaufgabe = major test; Stegreifaufgabe = surprise test
Grundwissen = core knowledge for later years
scenes.narration: The verbs: «erweitern», expand, «kürzen», reduce, and «vollständig gekürzt», fully reduced, the form many teachers expect for final answers. «Gleichnamig» means two fractions have the same denominator, and the smallest such denominator is the «Hauptnenner». Then the test words. A «Schulaufgabe» is a major written test, announced in advance and usually weighted more than a short test. A «Stegreifaufgabe», often just called «Ex», is a short unannounced test, usually on recent lessons. «Grundwissen» is core knowledge the school expects to stay available in later years. Fractions are usually counted as «Grundwissen».

scenes.question: Your child says: "Ich muss den Bruch noch kürzen." What do they have to do?
scenes.hint: Think of the picture with sixteen pieces becoming eight.
scenes.narration: A quick check for you. Your child looks at an answer and says: «Ich muss den Bruch noch kürzen». What do they have to do? Take a moment. You have heard the word a few times now, and the picture with the circle should help you.

bullets: kürzen = reduce the fraction
Divide top and bottom by the same number
6/16 → 3/8: now it is fully reduced
scenes.narration: «Kürzen» means to reduce. Your child divides the numerator and the denominator by the same number until no common divisor is left. Six sixteenths becomes three eighths, and three eighths is «vollständig gekürzt», fully reduced. Many teachers expect the final answer in this form, and depending on the teacher a correct but unreduced fraction can lose a point. The class exercise book shows what your child's teacher expects. If you want to help, ask: «Ist das vollständig gekürzt?» Is that fully reduced? Your child will know exactly what you mean.

chapters.title: Five typical mistakes
chapters.goal: You recognise the common mistakes and know how to correct them with a picture.

scenes.narration: Five mistakes are common in many classes, and all five are corrected by going back to a picture rather than repeating a rule. If you recognise which mistake your child made, you can ask the one question that fixes it. Here they are, two at a time, with the question to ask.

bullets: Unequal parts counted: a circle cut unevenly
Adding tops and bottoms: 1/2 + 1/3 ≠ 2/5
Correct is 5/6; adding comes later in the year
scenes.narration: Mistake one: counting parts that are not equal. A circle cut unevenly into four pieces does not show quarters. Ask: are all the pieces the same size? Mistake two: adding numerators and adding denominators. One half plus one third is not two fifths, it is five sixths. Adding fractions is a later topic, but children try it early. Ask: half a pizza plus a third of a pizza, is that really less than half? The picture ends the discussion.

bullets: False belief: 1/8 > 1/4 because 8 > 4
Crossing out digits: 16/64 = 1/4 by luck
Correction: more pieces, smaller pieces
scenes.narration: Mistake three: believing that a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction, so one eighth would be more than one quarter. Ask: a cake for eight people or for four, when is your piece bigger? The more pieces, the smaller each piece. Mistake four: reducing by crossing out digits. Sixteen over sixty-four gives one quarter if you cross out the sixes, but that is luck, not maths. Ask: which number did you divide top and bottom by? If there is no single answer, it was not «kürzen».

bullets: 3/4 of 20 € is right, but of what?
Backwards: 2/5 of the route = 6 km. Whole?
Correction: name the whole first, then calculate
scenes.narration: Mistake five often causes trouble in word problems: forgetting the whole, «das Ganze». Three quarters of twenty euros is fifteen euros, fine. But many tasks run backwards: two fifths of a route are six kilometres, how long is the route? Children who only know the forward direction get stuck. Ask: what is the whole here, and do we know it or are we looking for it? Once the whole is named, the calculation is usually short.

chapters.title: Helping at home, and what comes next
chapters.goal: You have a ten-minute routine that works without German, and you know what follows.

scenes.narration: You do not need German to help, and you do not need worksheets. Ten minutes a few times a week, in your own language, with the German words dropped in where the school uses them. Here is a routine that works in most families, and then a look at what the school checks and which topics come next.

bullets: Pizza, chocolate, cake: cut, share, name the fraction
Jug: 1/4 litre, 3/4 litre; clock: quarter hour
Tape measure as number line: where is 3/4 m?
scenes.narration: Step one: find fractions around the house and talk about them in your own language. Cut a pizza or a bar of chocolate and name the shares. Use a measuring jug: a quarter of a litre, three quarters of a litre. Use the clock: a quarter of an hour. A tape measure is a number line: where is three quarters of a metre? Then ask your child for the German word. They become the teacher, which is the best way to learn, and you pick up the vocabulary for free.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Steps 2 and 3: explain, then three tasks
bullets: Why are 3/8 and 6/16 the same amount?
Why is 1/8 smaller than 1/4?
Three tasks: a share, reduce or expand, compare
scenes.narration: Step two: let your child explain rather than quizzing them. Why are three eighths and six sixteenths the same amount? Why is one eighth smaller than one quarter? If they can explain it with a picture, in any language, they understand it. Step three: three short tasks, one of each kind. Find a share, such as three quarters of twelve apples. Reduce or expand a fraction fully. Compare two fractions, and as a bonus say that one half is fifty per cent. Three tasks, done well, beat twenty done in a hurry.

bullets: Read a share from a picture and draw one
Expand, reduce, find the common denominator
Order fractions and place them on the number line
Word problem: share of a whole, find the whole
scenes.narration: What do the tests on this topic usually check? Reading a share from a picture and drawing one. Expanding, reducing and finding the common denominator. Ordering fractions and placing them on the number line. And a word problem that asks for a share of a whole, or for the whole itself. In Bavaria the big written test is the «Schulaufgabe» and the short surprise test is the «Stegreifaufgabe». Which tasks appear, and how many, is decided by the teacher, so the class exercise book is the best guide.

scenes.onScreenTitle: Outlook: per cent is a fraction
scenes.narration: What comes next. Still in this topic, per cent, «Prozent», appears as another way of writing a fraction: twenty-five per cent is one quarter, so a quarter of two hundred euros is fifty euros. Then come decimals, «Dezimalbrüche», where the German school writes a decimal comma, zero comma two five, where English writes a point. Then adding and subtracting fractions, then multiplying and dividing. Full percentage calculation follows later, after area and volume. Every one of these rests on the four pictures from this video.

In short: you do not need German to help with fractions. Learn the handful of words, «Zähler», «Nenner», «erweitern», «kürzen», «Hauptnenner», and let your child explain the pictures to you in any language, and use the pizza, the jug and the tape measure at home. The German version of this guide and the lesson for children are on this channel. If a German school term puzzles you, write it in the comments and we will explain it. Subscribe for the next topic.
